annotations.text:
Three readings of "the programmer should possibly be a different view".

C is chosen: opening a cue Includes it, so the programmer IS the cue editor. A and B are kept for the record.

All three drop the Values / Layers / FX tabs — that follows from giving the programmer room, whichever structure wins.

Direction C at the app's real density — same tokens, same control heights, same ownership ring colours as ownershipCellClass().

Top row: the Programmer, and its action bar / source-strip states.
Middle: the Show view, and the show bar at four widths.
Bottom: the Look library, the template editor, and how colour resolves across fixture types.

Page 3 supersedes the layer and template thinking here — read it after this.

Dark-only on purpose: this is read at a desk in a blacked-out room.

Brief item 6 — the cue reads like the programmer.

The collapsed row carries a compressed strip of the cue's cooked output in the grid's own language: swatches for colour, bars for level. Expanded, it is the same grid and the same LayerRow, drawn read-only.

So there is no second cue editor to drift — CuePropsPane, TargetsPane and LayersPane's two arrangements all go.

Round 2, answering all four notes at once - because they turned out to be one.

Round 1 defined a template as "a Look whose rows are deferred", which is the data model talking, not a design. Split properly: a TEMPLATE composes values (one family, applied to a selection), a LOOK composes cues (any families, applied as a layer). That is what the missing New button was really about - it belongs on /templates, not /looks.

And the grid gets a SCOPE. Local values are just the top of the stack, so focusing a layer points the same grid at that Look. No jumping between library and cue.

Bottom row answers the two effect questions: where a new effect lands, and how a mixed values+FX Look gets built.

Start top-left.
